extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in aviation, safety, and current events
extracted.subtask_description: A short news article reporting on an in‑flight equipment failure (door plug blowout) and the responses from the airline, manufacturer, regulator, and investigators. Focuses on factual chronology, official statements, regulatory actions, and investigation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledging the mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing CEO: "we're going to approach this number one acknowledging our mistake."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The company should publicly acknowledge responsibility where appropriate as an initial response; the article quotes Calhoun stating this is the first approach to handling the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete transparency and cooperation with investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: "We're going to approach it with 100% and complete transparency every step of the way. We are going to work with the NTSB who is investigating the accident itself to find out what the cause is."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public messaging should commit to full transparency and active cooperation with the NTSB and other investigators; the article emphasizes Boeing's stated intent to be fully transparent and collaborative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory grounding until aircraft are demonstrated safe
rubrics_metrics.description: FAA: "every Boeing 737-9 Max with a plug door will remain grounded until the FAA finds each can safely return to operation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators may require a temporary grounding and explicit clearance before affected aircraft return to service; the FAA grounded 171 Boeing 737 Max 9s for safety inspections as reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety inspections and readiness actions required before return to service
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAA and Boeing noted inspections, procedures, and readiness actions must be put into place to ensure every next airplane that moves into the sky is safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspections (e.g., of door plugs and hardware) and institutional readiness are required steps; the CEO referenced inspections and procedural actions that must be completed to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer responsibility for installation/manufacturing issues
rubrics_metrics.description: United said it believes the loose hardware on its grounded planes is the result of an installation issue, which would be the manufacturer's responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evidence points to installation or manufacturing defects (loose bolts, hardware), liability and corrective action fall to manufacturers; the article cites airline statements attributing the problem to installation/manufacturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative focus on missing or loose bolts/hardware
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators are increasingly looking at four unaccounted-for bolts that should have kept the door panel from flying off during the flight; NTSB officials said they are not yet sure if the bolts ... "ever existed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough investigation should account for required fasteners and hardware, including whether they were present, installed correctly, or ever existed; the article highlights missing/loose bolts as a key investigative line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of prior warnings and system alerts
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilots had reported that the same plane experienced three pressurization warnings, from cockpit dashboard lights, between Dec. 7 and Jan. 4. At least one occurred in-flight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should factor prior warnings/alerts and maintenance history when determining root cause; the article notes earlier pressurization warnings on the aircraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew performance and training as critical safety factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Calhoun expressed "huge thanks and compliments" to the pilots and flight attendants who "got that airplane back on the ground" and said "they train their lives to do that."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should recognize crew actions and training effectiveness in emergency outcomes; the piece praises the crew's response as central to preventing serious injuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of event (accident vs. incident)
rubrics_metrics.description: NTSB chair Jennifer Homendy called Friday's event "an accident, not an incident."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How authorities classify an event affects investigative scope and public messaging — labeling it an accident signals greater gravity and formal investigative processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence recovery and chain-of-evidence (debris, passenger property)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lost door plug was discovered in a backyard; two cell phones sucked out of the plane were also found, one still working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery and documentation of physical evidence (debris, personal items) are important to reconstruction and investigation; the article documents location and condition of recovered items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential legal and litigation implications for suppliers
rubrics_metrics.description: A class-action lawsuit was brought against Spirit AeroSystems alleging products had "sustained quality failures" and "frequently contained defects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported quality failures can lead to litigation against suppliers; news reporting should note legal claims and their alleged basis when relevant to the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate assurance to prevent recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Calhoun: ensure all procedures are put into place, inspections, all the readiness actions that are required to ensure every next airplane that moves into the sky is in fact safe and that this event can never happen again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies often frame commitments to corrective measures and 'never again' assurances in public statements; reporting should capture these commitments and the concrete steps promised.
